newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters back to work at UPS by mid-week - Herman.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters back to work at UPS by mid-week - Herman.

text.p: Labor Secretary Alexis Herman said on Tuesday that Teamsters workers will return to their jobs at United Parcel Service by mid-week pending ratification of a tentative deal that ended the 15-day strike.

But Herman stopped short of saying whether she thought UPS would have to cut union jobs as the world's largest parcel delivery company had threatened to do last week if the strike did not end by a certain time.

"(Teamsters President) Ron Carey has indicated that he will be hard at work today to get this agreement ratified by his membership. As he has indicated and the company has indicated that by mid-week that the workers will start to return to work," she told NBC's "Today" program.
Asked how many jobs she predicted the company would have to cut, Herman responded: "I can't comment on the number of jobs that UPS will have to take into consideration, if any."

"Obviously that is a decision that the company will have to make. I think that the company is committed to trying to get all of their workers back to working again. I believe that will be their goal and exactly how they will do that is certainly a decision that the company will have to make."
UPS had warned striking workers it would lay off 15,000 when they returned because the strike had damaged its long-term business.
In a news conference held after the tentative agreement was reached, Carey conceded that the company would have to carry out at least some temporary layoffs.
The agreement, reached late on Monday evening, saw the union win on its key issue, the conversion of part-time jobs to full-time positions.
The union demanded and won the conversion of 10,000 jobs over the five-year life of the contract, while the company originally offered only 1,000, Carey said.
The agreement will phase out over six months the use of subcontractors, except during the crush of holiday package shipping, giving the jobs instead to UPS workers, he said.
The agreement was also a major victory for Herman. The labor secretary brought the parties back to the bargaining table on Thursday for marathon talks.
Negotiations lasted nearly 90 hours, with scant time off for sleep, until a deal was hammered out.

A clearly relieved Herman, when asked by NBC if her decision to stay in the same Washington hotel as the negotiators showed subtle pressure on her part, joked, "I wasn't trying to be subtle, I was being very direct. I moved in with them."
